content.prompt: In Mark’s account, the man saw unclearly at first; what happened after Jesus laid hands on his eyes again?
content.heading: A detail in Mark 8:22-26
content.scopeNote: This discovery describes what the cited passage says in the World English Bible.

sources.title: World English Bible (classic)
sources.excerpt: He came to Bethsaida. They brought a blind man to him, and begged him to touch him. He took hold of the blind man by the hand, and brought him out of the village. When he had spat on his eyes, and laid his hands on him, he asked him if he saw anything. He looked up, and said, “I see men; for I see them like trees walking.” Then again he laid his hands on his eyes. He looked intently, and was restored, and saw everyone clearly. He sent him away to his house, saying, “Don’t enter into the village, nor tell anyone in the village.”
sources.rights: World English Bible text is public domain. https://ebible.org/eng-web/copyright.htm

claims.text: After Jesus laid hands on him again, the man saw everyone clearly.
Jesus then sent him home and told him not to enter the village.

assessments.rationale: The prompt clearly establishes a man with initially unclear sight and Jesus touching his eyes again, without requiring church jargon. However, the tested fact is simply successful restoration after further healing. The passage's distinctive image of people resembling walking trees is not the discovery being tested. A player can favor complete restoration through ordinary expectations about a healing story, without biblical knowledge. The alternatives are parallel visual outcomes; restricted clarity and continued blurred sight are plausible incomplete-restoration guesses, but renewed blindness is a weak distractor. Total: 3/8; reject.

The scene is clear, concise, and free of unexplained church jargon. However, the potentially memorable connection—restoration occurring in stages—is supplied in the setup rather than discovered through the answer. The requested fact is merely the expected successful healing outcome. Everyday expectations strongly favor complete restoration over continued impairment or renewed blindness. Two limited-vision distractors are credible given the initial partial sight, but renewed blindness is weak. Total: 3/8; reject despite full textual accuracy.
